Where it began

Mitchell Marsh was born in Attadale on 20 October 1991 and grew up in Perth, where he went to Wesley College. Cricket ran in the house. His father, Geoff Marsh, and his older brother, Shaun, both played for Australia, and his sister, Melissa, played basketball professionally. As a teenager he was good enough at Australian football to represent Western Australia at the 2008 under-18 championships.

Cricket won. He first played for Western Australia at 17, in February 2009, at the time the youngest player ever to appear in an Australian domestic one-day match. A year later he captained Australia to victory at the 2010 Under-19 World Cup.

The player

His Test debut came against Pakistan in the United Arab Emirates in October 2014. Over 46 Tests between 2014 and 2024 he made 2,083 runs at 28.53, with 3 hundreds, and took 51 wickets at 40.41. His best bowling, 5 for 46, came in the last Test of the 2019 Ashes.

His first Test hundred, 181 against England in the 2017–18 Ashes, was a long time coming and worth the wait. Even better was Headingley in 2023. Back in the Test side for the first time since 2019, he walked in with Australia in trouble and hit 118 from 118 balls. In December 2023 he followed it with scores of 90, 63 not out and 96 against Pakistan.

What made him special

He hit the ball very hard and did not like to wait. In the shorter formats that made him a match-winner: he was part of the side that won the 2015 World Cup, was player of the match with 77 in the final of the 2021 T20 World Cup, and made 177 not out against Bangladesh at the 2023 World Cup, which Australia went on to win.

In Tests his runs tended to arrive in bursts rather than a steady stream. When a burst came, though, it usually came at a gallop.

Away from the middle

He won the Allan Border Medal in 2023, and that year he was made captain of Australia's T20 side. He played in the IPL for several teams, including Pune Warriors, then coached by his father, and in the Big Bash with Perth Scorchers.

A West Australian through and through, he nonetheless gave his football loyalty to North Melbourne.

And finally

Brothers keep score of everything. Mitch's 181 left him one run short of Shaun's career best of 182, so the bragging rights at Marsh family gatherings stayed with the elder brother, by the narrowest of margins.
